intuition: Use a queue to visit the shallowest nodes first. The first leaf you reach ends the shortest root-to-leaf path. Return its depth immediately. A node with one missing child is not a leaf, so an empty child must not be mistaken for a shorter finished path.

The endpoint must be a real leaf: a node with neither child. A missing left child beside an existing right child is not a completed path. This distinction is why simply taking the smaller of two child depths can fail when one subtree is absent.

Queue each node with its depth in nodes, starting at one for the root. FIFO traversal visits nondecreasing depths; therefore the first leaf popped has the minimum possible depth. Existing children receive depth+1. An empty input is separate and returns zero because there is no root-to-leaf path.

steps: Remove 3. It has children, so it is not a leaf; append (9,2) followed by (20,2).
Remove (9,2). Both child references are absent, making 9 a genuine leaf.
Because the queue processes depth 2 before any deeper frontier, no leaf with a smaller depth can still be undiscovered.
Return 2 immediately. Node 20 and its depth-3 children do not need to be processed to prove this answer.

codeNotes.note: Depth counts nodes on the path, so the root contributes one. Storing depth beside each queued node avoids separately managing level counters.

codeNotes.note: Both absences are required. A one-child node must continue down its existing branch rather than treating a missing subtree as a shorter path.
An existing child extends the path by exactly one node. Its queued depth is therefore its parent depth plus one.

keyDecision: A leaf has neither a left child nor a right child. Count depth in nodes.
